For each row, the kernel could launch multiple blocks. Each block wrote its top-K candidates to scratch memory, incremented a per-row counter, and the last block merged the candidate lists. Recording summary

The agent wrote a single-file implementation whose stated design was:

grid = rows * S blocks (S = splits per row, power of two).
each block reads its chunk with float4 loads, sorts 8 elements per thread
in registers, builds sorted-descending K-segments in shared memory with
a bitonic network, then reduces segments pairwise with the classic
"elementwise max of A[i], B[K-1-i] then bitonic-merge" top-K trick.
if S == 1 the block writes the row result directly. Otherwise blocks write
their sorted K-list candidates to global scratch; the last block to finish
a row (atomic counter) merges the S sorted lists and writes the output.

The implementation padded K to a power of two, selected a split count based on row count and chunk size, and used float4 loads when n was divisible by four. It filled invalid entries with negative infinity, sorted per-thread groups of eight, merged candidate segments in shared memory, then wrote either final outputs or scratch candidates.

Memory summary

The reconstructed final solution is a custom CUDA C++ extension embedded in solution.py. It sorts chunks in registers, keeps sorted top-k candidate lists in shared memory, and merges them; split rows use scratch buffers and an atomic counter so the last block merges the row’s candidate lists. The run passed a three-trial smoke test on each of the five target shapes. There is no official correctness result or benchmark score in the available artifacts, and the run is marked unaudited.

Each block loads up to eight values per thread, sorts them in registers, and uses a bitonic merge tree in shared memory. For split rows, blocks write their top-k candidates to scratch storage; the last block to finish merges those lists and writes the output.
